articles.title: Internal DOJ charts show agency bleeding staff as caseloads surge
articles.summary: A drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads, according to documents obtained by The Hill and...
articles.body:
A drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads, according to documents obtained by The Hill and NewsNation.

A series of charts, apparently inadvertently shared and then recalled, show how the number of attorneys within the civil division has plummeted under the Trump administration.

The charts substantiate a dynamic long suspected: that the Department of Justice (DOJ) would not be able to swiftly replace a crew of veteran attorneys after a wave of firings and resignations.

Stacey Young, who founded the DOJ alumni group Justice Connection, described the staff turnover as a "massive exodus."

"The workload has skyrocketed, particularly in the civil division offices that have lost the most lawyers. So what we're seeing is that the lawyers who are left are overworked, stressed out, many have lost those who led their office because they were pushed out by this administration. And because of the difficult circumstances under which they're working, I expect that the rate of departures won't slow down anytime soon," she told The Hill.

"Putting out this data seems to me like a desperate cry for help. It seems like the civil division knows how badly it needs more funds to hire more lawyers to make up for the purge of longstanding experts that they caused."

According to the Office of Personnel Management, the Justice Department has lost roughly 10,000 workers since the start of the Trump administration, a metric that includes component agencies like the FBI and the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

In graph after graph, the charts track data from the start of the Trump administration through August, showing a significant decline in civil division staff as caseloads have steadily ticked up.

DOJ defended the workload, saying it has hired new staff.

"The Civil Division is working every day to advance and defend the President's agenda in court, and it is winning. Since the start of this Administration, the Civil Division has hired over 200 new attorneys with many more in the pipeline," a spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill.

"Civil Division attorneys have achieved countless wins in courts across the country and secured billions of dollars in fraud recoveries for the American people," they added.

One chart reviewing impact on each branch within the division detailed how caseload was skyrocketing — with work for the commercial litigation branch jumping a whopping 84 percent per attorney, while lawyers in the Office of Immigration Litigation saw their workload jump 63 percent.

Attorneys who work on appeals saw their caseloads jump 54 percent while lawyers in the federal programs branch — those who work on defending executive orders among other administration priorities — saw their workloads jump 44 percent.

The number of attorneys in the federal programs branch dropped from 113 to 71 just within the first few months of the Trump administration. A jump in cases has largely settled to around 1,000, but they are being handled by a diminished team.

Jennifer Ricketts, a former Justice Department attorney who led the federal programs branch, said the swift exodus shows how many longtime attorneys who defended presidential priorities across administrations likely began looking for a new job as soon as President Trump won the election.

"They were aware of how much in the first Trump administration they tried to stretch the law and put us in positions where we struggled to make sure we satisfied our professional responsibilities and folks did not want to have to go through that exercise again," she said of the branch.

"You don't get jobs really quickly. So they had already started looking after the election, so it was not tied to any specific decision. It was the anticipation of what they may do, especially given how aggressive they said they were going to be and how aggressive we had seen them be in Trump one …. I think folks knew maybe not the scope of what was coming, but they knew none of it was going to be pleasant."

One of the other most significant declines in staffing — combined with one of the highest rises in cases — was in the Office of Immigration Litigation, which has seen cases surge amid Trump's pledge to carry out the largest mass deportation operation in history.

The Office of Immigration Litigation handles both individual immigration cases being heard at the Board of Immigration Appeals as well as immigration matters brought in federal district court, such as habeas corpus cases brought by migrants being held in detention. Habeas petitions have soared alongside detention rates as the administration has largely cut off access to bond hearings.

One former staffer from the immigration office noted the steady decline in staff in that branch, with attorneys going from 320 down to 243 as cases climbed from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500.

"We never had attrition like we've had. There's been a lot of reasons for that," the former staffer said.

Early in the administration, the Justice Department moved the branch's leader to a new sanctuary city task force, and the Justice Department later made headlines for firing Erez Reuveni, a longtime Office of Immigration Litigation staffer, after he acknowledged in court that Kilmar Abrego Garcia had been mistakenly deported.

"When our colleague Erez Reuveni got fired, I think there were a lot of people that were saying, 'If that could happen to him that could happen to any of us,'" the former staffer continued. "And I think that people just started looking, and you know, workload's gone up. The office has sort of tried to recover from those blows … But it's been increasingly challenging for people to do that. I think there's a lot of unhappy people."

"With caseload going up and the resources going down, it just makes it challenging," they added.

Also surprising is the attrition among appellate staff attorneys, though their ranks have been rising over the last several months.

"It's a very plum section, very elite section, and if folks leave there, they would often go to the solicitor general's office or some other very prestigious placement," Ricketts said, referencing the team of attorneys for the solicitor who argue before the Supreme Court.

While staffing in that branch hasn't dipped as much as others, their caseload has increased substantially because the Trump administration has been appealing so many of its losses in court.

Though now down six attorneys from the 61 it began with, the number of appealed cases went from around 780 at the start of the administration to more than 1,100 last month.

"They will appeal everything. I mean, it does not appear to be an administration that takes losses. They do not seem to be worried about creating bad law in the court of appeals. They seem to be pursuing a very aggressive interpretation of executive branch authority, and so they are willing to roll the dice and take it up," Ricketts said.

"I think my sense is they have a sense that the Supreme Court is willing to accept more of those ideas, what would have been considered extreme ideas, than we ever imagined, and so why not?"

Similarly to the Office of Immigration Litigation, the commercial litigation branch has also seen a consistent loss in staff — dropping from 350 at the start of the administration down to 289 — while caseloads have jumped from around 13,000 to nearly 19,000.

It's hard to know what has driven the surge in caseload in the branch, which handles a wide variety of matters from cases where the government has a financial interest to intellectual property to those who represent the U.S. in cases in foreign courts.

But it does include two areas where there has been more active litigation.

The commercial litigation branch includes fraud — a topic of great interest to the Trump administration as it probes entitlement programs.

It also handles cases before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the quasi judicial board responsible for reviewing federal employee workplace challenges, including wrongful termination cases that have surged as the Trump administration pushed to reduce the size of the government.

Making its case in a mistakenly shared email

After the email with the charts was sent last week, it was quickly recalled.

Sources suspect the graphs are preparation for the next budget cycle.

"Somewhere along the line, somebody in the division or the department is going to use this data to justify asking for more resources," the former Office of Immigration Litigation staffer said.

They noted that none of the graphs start its axis at zero, a choice that emphasizes the rise in cases and fall in staff.

"They ginned up the charts to make that visually apparent," they said.

The Justice Department has already made efforts to recruit more staff. In May, the department promised something largely unheard of in the federal government — a $25,000 signing bonus to those joining the civil division.

"DOJ had never given signing bonuses to try to attract applicants. These jobs were some of the most competitive legal jobs in the field. The fact that they're now having to provide financial incentives for people to apply shows you just how desperate they are," Young said.

"And we know that job openings that used to attract hundreds or thousands of applications are now attracting almost none."

The Justice Department took a number of actions shortly after Trump took office that flushed staff and prompted headlines.

In the criminal division, the Justice Department fired those who had worked on cases involving Trump. In the civil division, many branch leaders were reassigned to take on unrelated work. The U.S. pardon attorney lost her job after she refused to certify that actor Mel Gibson should have his gun rights restored. And still more attorneys sought and gained jobs outside the department or availed themselves of a government buyout spearheaded by Elon Musk.

At the beginning of the administration, the Justice Department also withdrew offers to recent graduates who had been given entry level jobs through the prestigious Attorney General's Honors Program, cutting off a pipeline of young attorneys from top schools who then rise through the ranks of the department.

"It reflects what we've been saying all along. This situation is untenable when you have an office that is experiencing a surge of cases because of this administration's lawless conduct at a time when lawyers are fleeing the department. The administration won't be able to defend itself in court," Young said.

"DOJ lawyers, in the best of times, are overworked. Their workloads right now have increased exponentially, especially when it comes to civil division lawyers, and as their workloads continue to increase, more will leave, and the problem will just keep getting worse and worse."

articles.title: Trump said he would campaign in midterm battlegrounds. He's starting in deep red states instead
articles.summary: President Donald Trump vowed to campaign in 35 of the most competitive battleground races in the final sprint to November's midterm elections.  Instead, he w...
articles.body:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (AP) — President Donald Trump vowed to campaign in 35 of the most competitive battleground races in the final sprint to November's midterm elections .

Instead, he will begin October by stumping in Alabama and Oklahoma, two of the most Republican states in the nation. His events are sure to draw enthusiastic crowds of fans, but his choice of destinations is a reminder of his deep unpopularity in much of the country during a campaign season he's sought to make all about himself.

Trump will hold rallies next week in Durant, Oklahoma, and Mobile, Alabama, where he is sure to draw crowds, but he has also raised eyebrows.

While organizers insist the rallies are in locations with media markets that span state lines and they will help bolster broader turnout, Trump's itinerary is yet another sign of the uphill fight that his party faces. Republicans have already been pouring money into red states once considered safe as they try to shore up candidates facing an unhappy electorate that has soured on Trump and his policies.

Some Republicans have also been distancing themselves from the president in recent weeks as they try to appeal to voters beyond Trump's "Make America Great Again" base. They have removed or downplayed references to the president on their websites and increasingly voiced opposition to his unpopular war with Iran.

But Trump's events — Thursday in Durant and Friday in Mobile — are also likely to deliver something else he craves: adoring crowds. He is almost guaranteed to fill the venues with the kind of die-hard supporters who fueled his political rise, projecting excitement as he tries to bolster enthusiasm and rally Republicans.

"The President's ability to engage with and activate low-propensity voters is unmatched. That's why he'll be barnstorming the country to activate the voters we need to win in November," said Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre, promising more October rallies to come.

Democrats, meanwhile, celebrated the announcement. "The political floor is falling out from underneath Trump and Congressional Republicans, forcing them to scramble to spend and campaign in deep red territory in the final weeks," said Viet Shelton, spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans expect Trump's appeal to cross state lines

The RNC noted that Durant, Oklahoma, is on the Texas border and next to the Dallas-Fort Worth media market, and will draw Republicans in Texas, which has emerged as one of the most critical states on the map. Scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom Trump backed over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, is locked in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico . Gov. Greg Abbott is also facing a stronger-than-expected challenger in Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Mobile is next to Florida's panhandle, a Republican stronghold where high turnout can help bolster Trump-backed candidates running for Senate and governor. However, Florida Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is not expected to attend.

In Oklahoma, Trump will be stumping for Mike Mazzei, whom he backed as the Republican nominee for governor during a competitive primary . Mazzei is running against Oklahoma's Democratic House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson.

"This race continues to get more competitive — and national Republicans are right to be worried about Mazzei," Democratic Governors Association spokesperson Kevin Donohoe said in a statement.

Alabama, meanwhile, holds deep nostalgia for Trump and his early supporters. He held his first mega-rally in Mobile more than a decade ago, drawing some 30,000 people to a college football stadium. The crowd made clear to skeptics of his campaign that he was more than a celebrity novelty.

"I think it's very natural that he would host a rally here as he is gearing up for the midterm elections," said John Wahl, the Republican candidate for lieutenant governor and former chair of the Alabama Republican Party.

Although Republicans remain the heavy favorites in Alabama's statewide campaigns, they face a more challenging political landscape this year.

Former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones is mounting a vigorous campaign for Alabama governor against one of Trump's most vocal allies, Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who said he welcomed the president's visit .

Republican Rep. Barry Moore, running to replace Tuberville in the Senate with Trump's backing, said the president's rally "will be the jet fuel we need to win big in Alabama."

Mobile is also near Alabama's 2nd Congressional District, which leans red after its lines were redrawn but is not a slam dunk for Republicans as they try to dislodge Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures.

Figures has been criticizing the president's plan to lower import tariffs on foreign beef in an appeal to cattle ranchers as he tries to fend off a challenge from his Trump-backed opponent, State Rep. Rhett Marques.

Trump has promised to ramp up his campaigning in the election's final stretch and had said he would visit all of the most competitive districts.

"It's all about 35 races," he said at a recent Rose Garden dinner attended by Republican lawmakers. "I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places and we're going to see if we can get everyone elected."

Ohio Republican Party Chairman Alex Triantafilou said he hoped Trump would visit his state, where he won in 2024 by 11 percentage points. Republican Sen. John Husted is facing a competitive challenge from Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

"We definitely want him here," Triantafilou said. "He's a turnout driver for us."

Colvin reported from New York. Associated Press reporters Bill Barrow in Atlanta and Thomas Beaumont in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

articles.title: Meia Maratona Praia Grande altera trânsito e ônibus neste domingo | G1
articles.standfirst: Prova provoca bloqueios em duas importantes avenidas e altera o itinerário de seis linhas de ônibus. Interdições começam às 4h e devem terminar às 11h.
articles.summary: Prova provoca bloqueios em duas importantes avenidas e altera o itinerário de seis linhas de ônibus. Interdições começam às 4h e devem terminar às 11h.
articles.body:
Meia Maratona Tribuna irá afetar vias e linhas de transporte público em Praia Grande (SP). — Foto: Divulgação/Prefeitura de Praia Grande

A 14ª Meia Maratona Tribuna vai movimentar Praia Grande, no litoral de São Paulo, neste domingo (27). A realização da prova também provocará mudanças no trânsito, com interdições em duas importantes avenidas e alterações no itinerário de seis linhas de ônibus ( confira abaixo ).

Os bloqueios começam às 4h e têm previsão de liberação às 11h. Segundo a Secretaria de Trânsito (Setran), as interdições serão realizadas para garantir a segurança dos atletas durante a prova.

A Avenida Presidente Castelo Branco ficará bloqueada entre a Rua Salvador Molinari, no Caiçara, e a Rua Gaspar Vianna, no Canto do Forte.

Na Avenida Presidente Kennedy, a interdição será entre a Rua 1º de Janeiro e a Rua Gilberto Fouad Beck, no bairro Mirim.

Linha 11PR (sentido Solemar/Terminal Tático/Terminal Tude Bastos) – segue pela Avenida Presidente Kennedy, Rua Gilberto Fouad Beck, Avenida Doutor Roberto de Almeida Vinhas, Rua José Borges Neto, Terminal Tático, Rua 23 de Outubro e Avenida 31 de Março. Depois, retorna à Avenida Presidente Kennedy e segue pelas avenidas Guilhermina e Brasil, retomando o itinerário normal pela Rua Pernambuco.

Linha 11PR (sentido Terminal Tude Bastos/Terminal Tático/Solemar) – segue pelas avenidas Presidente Costa e Silva, Brasil e Guilhermina até a Presidente Kennedy. Depois, passa pela Rua 1º de Janeiro, Terminal Tático, ruas José Borges Neto, Moisés Cardoso de Oliveira, Valter José Alves, Jorge Monteiro dos Santos e Rosa Marli de Souza, retornando à Avenida Presidente Kennedy.

Linha 12CO (sentido Terminal Tático/Terminal Tude Bastos) – segue pelas ruas José Borges Neto e 23 de Outubro e pelas avenidas 31 de Março e Presidente Kennedy. Faz o retorno na rotatória da Rua Guimarães Rosa e segue no sentido Solemar, retomando o itinerário normal pela Avenida Dom Pedro II.

Linha 15SO (sentido Terminal Tático/Solemar) – segue pelas ruas José Borges Neto, Moisés Cardoso de Oliveira, Valter José Alves, Jorge Monteiro dos Santos e Rosa Marli de Souza, acessando a Avenida Presidente Kennedy e retomando o itinerário pela Rua Marquês de Herval.

Linha 15SO (sentido Solemar/Terminal Tático) – segue pela Avenida Presidente Kennedy, Rua Marquês de Herval, Rua Gilberto Fouad Beck, Avenida Doutor Roberto de Almeida Vinhas e Rua José Borges Neto até o Terminal Tático.

Linha 17SA (sentido Terminal Tático/Terminal Tude Bastos) – segue pelas ruas José Borges Neto e 23 de Outubro e pela Avenida 31 de Março, retomando o itinerário normal pela Avenida Presidente Kennedy.

Linha 17SA (sentido Terminal Tude Bastos/Terminal Tático) – segue pelas avenidas Presidente Costa e Silva e Brasil, Rua Emancipador Paulo Fefim, Avenida Presidente Kennedy, Rua 1º de Janeiro e Terminal Tático. Depois, passa pelas ruas Valter José Alves, Jorge Monteiro dos Santos e Rosa Marli de Souza, retornando à Avenida Presidente Kennedy.

Linha 22ME (sentido Terminal Tático/Melvi) – segue pelas ruas José Borges Neto, Moisés Cardoso de Oliveira, Valter José Alves, Jorge Monteiro dos Santos e Rosa Marli de Souza, retomando o itinerário normal pela Avenida Presidente Kennedy.

Linha 94BF (sentido Terminal Tude Bastos/Forte) – segue pela Avenida do Trabalhador, Avenida Presidente Costa e Silva e Rua Jaú, retomando o itinerário normal.

casa  | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima de 55 anos sofreu traumatismos em diferentes partes do corpo, foi encaminhada para a Santa Casa de Martinópolis e transferida para um hospital em Presidente Prudente (SP).
articles.summary: Um homem de 55 anos ficou gravemente ferido após ser atingido por uma parede que desabou durante uma obra de demolição, na manhã deste sábado (26), em Martinópolis (SP).
articles.body:
Homem fica gravemente ferido após parede desabar durante demolição de imóvel em Martinópolis — Foto: Reprodução

Um homem de 55 anos ficou gravemente ferido após ser atingido por uma parede que desabou durante a demolição de uma casa, na manhã deste sábado (26), no Conjunto Habitacional Pedro e Zulmira, em Martinópolis (SP).

De acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros, a vítima trabalhava na residência quando foi atingida por uma das paredes.

O trabalhador sofreu traumatismos em diferentes partes do corpo. Após ser retirado do local, ele recebeu os primeiros atendimentos e foi encaminhado para a Santa Casa de Martinópolis.

Por causa da gravidade dos ferimentos, os socorristas solicitaram a transferência do paciente para um hospital em Presidente Prudente (SP).

Equipes da Brigada Municipal também auxiliaram no resgate e na imobilização da vítima. Até a última atualização, não havia novas informações sobre o estado de saúde do homem.

articles.title: Acidente na BR-174: 12 feridos são transferidos para Manaus | G1
articles.standfirst: Veículo perdeu o controle e caiu em uma ribanceira de aproximadamente 15 metros, em Presidente Figueiredo. Vídeo mostra desespero dos passageiros logo após o acidente.
articles.summary: Acidente na BR-174 em Presidente Figueiredo deixa feridos graves e mobiliza resgate após micro-ônibus cair em uma ribanceira de 15 metros.
articles.body:
Doze pessoas feridas após um micro-ônibus cair em uma ribanceira na BR-174 , em Presidente Figueiredo , no interior do Amazonas, foram transferidas para Manaus para receber atendimento especializado. Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Amazonas (CBMAM), três delas apresentavam estado mais grave.

O acidente aconteceu por volta das 8h deste sábado (26), no quilômetro 146 da rodovia, no sentido Manaus–Boa Vista. O micro-ônibus perdeu o controle e caiu em uma ribanceira de aproximadamente 15 metros.

Um vídeo gravado por um dos passageiros logo após o acidente mostra o desespero das pessoas que estavam no veículo . Nas imagens, passageiros aparecem feridos e assustados. Em determinado momento, uma mulher é vista carregando uma criança de colo.

Segundo o CBMAM, 22 pessoas receberam atendimento pré-hospitalar no local e, em seguida, foram encaminhadas ao Hospital Municipal Heraldo Neves, em Presidente Figueiredo. Entre os atendidos estão três crianças.

Do total de vítimas atendidas, 12 foram transferidas para Manaus para atendimento especializado. Três estavam em estado mais grave .

Ainda de acordo com os bombeiros, não houve registro de passageiros presos às ferragens.

O g1 procurou a Secretaria de Estado de Saúde do Amazonas (SES-AM) para saber se as vítimas transferidas para Manaus já foram atendidas e qual é o estado de saúde dos feridos. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não houve retorno.

A ocorrência mobilizou dez militares do Corpo de Bombeiros, três viaturas da corporação e equipes do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu).

O acidente aconteceu no quilômetro 146 da BR-174, trecho da rodovia que liga Manaus a Boa Vista.

articles.title: Torneio de pesca reúne competidores em balneário de Prudente | G1
articles.standfirst: Evento será realizado em novembro e terá modalidades de pesca embarcada e de barranco. Inscrições são gratuitas por formulário online.
articles.summary: Quem gosta de pesca esportiva já pode se programar para participar do Torneio de Pesca 2026, no Balneário da Amizade, em Presidente Prudente (SP). As inscrições já estão abertas.
articles.body:
Torneio de pesca reúne competidores em balneário de Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Prefeitura de Presidente Prudente/Divulgação

Quem gosta de pesca esportiva já pode se programar para participar do Torneio de Pesca 2026, no Balneário da Amizade, em Presidente Prudente (SP).

As inscrições já estão abertas e devem ser feitas por meio de um formulário online . O evento será realizado no dia 8 de novembro (um domingo), das 6h às 11h, e terá modalidades de pesca embarcada e de barranco.

A pesca embarcada será realizada em embarcações sem motor, movidas a remo ou pedal . Já a modalidade de barranco será disputada às margens do balneário , no lado de Presidente Prudente.

A competição é aberta ao público e terá pesca exclusivamente de tucunarés, seguindo o sistema de “pesque e solte” (os peixes capturados deverão ser devolvidos à água em boas condições).

A classificação será definida pelo comprimento do maior tucunaré capturado por cada participante, medido em centímetros, do focinho até a ponta da cauda. Em caso de empate, será considerado vencedor o competidor de maior idade.

Os três primeiros colocados receberão troféus e prêmios especiais, que serão definidos pela organização e pelos parceiros do evento.

Na modalidade embarcada, será obrigatório o uso de colete salva-vidas durante toda a prova. O equipamento deve ser providenciado pelo próprio participante .

Os pescadores também deverão apresentar licença para pesca amadora dentro do prazo de validade.

articles.title: Acidente na BR-174: Vídeo mostra micro-ônibus em ribanceira no AM | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagens foram feitas logo após o acidente e mostram passageiros feridos e assustados nas proximidades do veículo. O acidente aconteceu neste sábado (26), no quilômetro 146 da BR-174, em Presidente Figueiredo.
articles.summary: Acidente na BR-174 deixa 17 feridos após micro-ônibus cair em ribanceira no Amazonas; imagens mostram o socorro às vítimas em Presidente Figueiredo.
articles.body:
Um vídeo gravado por um dos passageiros mostra o desespero das pessoas após um micro-ônibus capotar e cair em uma ribanceira de aproximadamente 15 metros na manhã deste sábado (26), no quilômetro 146 da BR-174, em Presidente Figueiredo , no interior do Amazonas. ( veja acima ).

As imagens foram feitas logo após o acidente e mostram passageiros feridos e assustados nas proximidades do veículo. Em um dos momentos, uma mulher aparece carregando uma criança de colo.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Amazonas (CBMAM), 17 pessoas ficaram feridas e precisaram de atendimento médico . Entre as vítimas estão três crianças.

O acidente aconteceu por volta das 8h, no sentido Manaus –Boa Vista. Segundo os bombeiros, o micro-ônibus perdeu o controle antes de sair da pista e cair na ribanceira.

As vítimas receberam atendimento pré-hospitalar no local e foram encaminhadas ao Hospital Municipal Eraldo Neves, em Presidente Figueiredo. Não houve registro de passageiros presos às ferragens.

Ainda de acordo com o CBMAM, três vítimas em estado mais grave estavam sendo transferidas para Manaus . Elas devem receber atendimento especializado no Hospital e Pronto-Socorro João Lúcio.

O g1 procurou a Secretaria de Estado de Saúde do Amazonas (SES-AM) para saber se as vítimas já haviam sido recebidas na capital e qual é o estado de saúde delas, mas até a última atualização desta reportagem, não obteve retorno.

A ocorrência mobilizou dez militares do Corpo de Bombeiros, três viaturas da corporação e equipes do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu).

articles.title: Camilo Duarte propõe aumento do salário mínimo na Paraíba | G1
articles.standfirst: Em entrevista para à TV Cabo Branco, o candidato do Partido da Causa Operária falou ter interesse em aumentar o piso salarial do estado.
articles.summary: Em entrevista à TV Cabo Branco, o candidato do PCO, Camilo Duarte, afirmou que o salário atual não garante dignidade e defendeu o aumento do piso na Paraíba.
articles.body:
Camilo Duarte em entrevista à TV Cabo Branco — Foto: Reprodução TV Cabo Branco.

O candidato do Partido da Causa Operária (PCO) ao governo da Paraíba, Camilo Duarte, defendeu o aumento do piso salarial no estado. A declaração foi dada durante entrevista à TV Cabo Branco .

"Até pessoas com custo superior não têm perspectiva, porque você ganhar um salário mínimo ou pouco mais do que isso não é uma perspectiva".

Para defender a proposta, o candidato citou um levantamento do Departamento Intersindical de Estatística e Estudos Socioeconômicos (Dieese), que defende um valor maior para o salário mínimo no país.

"O salário mínimo atual é menos de um terço do que o DIES, que é um órgão ligado ao governo, disse que deveria ser o mínimo. Não é garantido a dignidade, qualquer perspectiva, para a imensa maioria da população".

articles.title: The media battle behind Brazil’s election
articles.summary: A corruption scandal, Bolsonaro’s comeback, and Trump’s influence collide as Brazil heads into elections.
articles.body:
As Brazilians head into national elections, there’s a familiar name on the ballot: Bolsonaro. Not former President Jair Bolsonaro. It’s his son Flavio, who is presenting himself to the electorate as a more moderate version of his father.

Election coverage has been dominated by a major corruption scandal – the biggest banking fraud case in the country’s history. Brazilians are accustomed to corruption scandals involving political figures. The coverage tends to be framed as: they’re all equally corrupt.

Contributors: Andrew Fishman – President & co-founder, Intercept Brasil David Nemer – Professor, University of Virginia Andre Pagliarini – Professor, Louisiana State University Natalia Portinari – Reporter, O Globo

On our radar: Donald Trump’s decision to bar three news outlets from the White House appears to have backfired after journalists organised a media boycott and a judge overturned the ban. Tariq Nafi has been tracking the latest duel between the US president and the media.

A fringe neo-Nazi movement in Spain, Nucleo Nacional, has attracted a growing online following by packaging incendiary and slickly produced content. The mainstream media attention the group has received has made a marginal organisation appear far larger and more influential than it is. The Listening Post’s Elettra Scrivo travels to Madrid – where she comes face-to-face with Nucleo Nacional’s members – to look at the reality that lies behind the spectacle.

Featuring: Miquel Ramos – Author, ‘Antifascistas’ Urszula Mrozowska – Digital researcher in hate speech and extremism

articles.title: Marqueteiro de candidato ao Senado morre após cirurgia no coração | G1

articles.summary: Informação foi confirmada por Lunelli antes da participação dele no debate dos candidatos ao Senado, promovido pela NSC TV.
articles.body:
Empresário e marqueteiro candidato ao Senado morre dias após cirurgia no coração em SC — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Morreu na sexta-feira (25), aos 48 anos, o empresário Elias Raasch , que atuava como marqueteiro na campanha de Antídio Lunelli (MDB), candidato ao Senado por Santa Catarina nas Eleições de 2026. Ele havia passado por uma cirurgia no coração .

A informação pelo candidato antes da participação dele no debate dos candidatos ao Senado, promovido pela NSC TV . Durante o encontro, Lunelli também lamentou a morte do amigo.

Raasch estava internado há cerca de uma semana no Hospital São José, em Jaraguá do Sul, no Norte de Santa Catarina, onde fez um procedimento de ponte de safenao .

Lunelli soube da morte do marqueteiro horas antes de participar do debate, que começou por volta das 23h. Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, o candidato também lamentou a morte.

"Elias acompanhou minha trajetória política desde o início. Foi responsável por todas as minhas campanhas. Essa foto, inclusive, foi tirada há um mês atrás quando estávamos em Criciúma", escreveu.

articles.title: Reprovação dos ministros do STF atinge 47%, recorde no Datafolha | G1
articles.standfirst: Outros 18% acham o trabalho dos ministros ótimo ou bom, e 31% como regular. Pesquisa tem margem de erro de dois pontos percentuais.
articles.summary: A reprovação dos ministros do STF chegou a 47% no Datafolha, que também aponta apoio majoritário à criação de um código de ética para a Corte.
articles.body:
Sessão plenária extraordinária do STF - 15/09/2026 — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada neste sábado (26) revelou que 47% dos brasileiros avaliam o trabalho dos ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) como negativo. Esse é o índice mais alto da série histórica iniciada em 2019 .

A avaliação positiva dos ministros é de 18%, atingindo o nível mais baixo desde 2019. Outros 31% classificam a atuação da Corte como regular e 4% não opinaram.

Os números também registraram que, entre eleitores de Lula (PT), 32% consideram o trabalho dos ministros como ótimo ou bom, e entre eleitores de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), o número é de 6%.

Já a avaliação negativa da Corte fica em 69% dos eleitores de Flávio, que classificam o trabalho dos ministros como ruim ou péssimo. No caso dos votantes de Lula, o número é de 24%.

Entre os entrevistados, 33% afirmam que a atuação dos ministros mais prejudica do que beneficia a candidatura do representante do PL, enquanto 23% apontam que as ações da Corte mais prejudicam do que beneficiam o candidato petista.

Sobre a proposta de criação de um Código de Ética e Conduta para os ministros do STF, defendida pelo presidente da Corte, Edson Fachin, 45% do eleitorado se diz a favor e 33%, contra.

Presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin em sessão plenária extraordinária do STF - 15/09/2026 — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

No início do ano, Fachin anunciou Cármen Lúcia como relatora da proposta de um Código de Ética para a Corte e disse que apresentou sugestões para a relatora.

"Um código de ética tem também um componente, digamos, de natureza material, histórico, cultural. Ele é também um conjunto de práticas. E só o debate sobre esta ideia já é relevante para aventar determinadas circunstâncias e, portanto, nós, a rigor, já começamos em várias circunstâncias, em vários quadrantes, a evidenciar interrogações, interpelações que os fatos geram sobre determinados tipos de eventos aqui."

A pesquisa, contratada por Folha e Globo, foi realizada de terça (22) a quarta (23) com 2.002 eleitores por meio de abordagem pessoal em pontos de fluxo populacional. A margem de erro máxima prevista é de 2 pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos, considerando um nível de confiança de 95%. Os dados constam no sistema do TSE (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral). O número de registro é BR-00304/2026.

articles.title: Morcegos com raiva são encontrados mortos em Marabá Paulista | G1
articles.standfirst: Três morcegos foram localizados caídos perto da ESF Nazaré, no Assentamento André Franco. Este é o primeiro caso registrado na cidade em 2026.
articles.summary: Três morcegos que testaram positivo para raiva foram encontrados mortos em Marabá Paulista (SP), neste sábado (26).
articles.body:
Centro de Controle de Zoonoses de Marabá Paulista (SP) — Foto: Prefeitura de Marabá Paulista/Divulgação

Três morcegos testaram positivo para raiva após serem encontrados mortos em Marabá Paulista (SP). A confirmação foi divulgada neste sábado (26) pela Secretaria Municipal de Saúde (SMS).

Segundo a pasta, os animais foram encontrados próximos à ESF Nazaré, no Assentamento André Franco. Este é o primeiro caso de morcegos com raiva registrado na cidade em 2026.

Profissionais de saúde localizaram os animais caídos nas proximidades da unidade de atendimento médico à população e acionaram a equipe de zoonoses para removê-los do local. As três amostras foram encaminhadas para análise e tiveram resultado positivo para raiva.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia registro de moradores que tivessem tido contato com os morcegos.

A pasta ainda informou que, após reunião técnica com os órgãos estaduais de Vigilância Epidemiológica e Sanitária, a SMS vai intensificar, a partir de segunda-feira (28), as ações de busca e de vacinação.

Orientações também serão reforçadas aos moradores, especialmente por meio das redes sociais, para que, em caso de contato com os animais, eles procurem imediatamente uma unidade de saúde.

Uma ação para intensificar a vacinação antirrábica para cães e gatos no Assentamento André Franco também será realizada como medida de prevenção.

"A SMS orienta a população a não tocar ou manipular morcegos, vivos ou mortos. Reforçamos que a presença de morcegos em seu habitat natural, por si só, não significa que o animal esteja doente ou ofereça risco. No entanto, caso seja encontrado um morcego caído no chão, morto, em local incomum ou apresentando comportamento anormal, não tente capturá-lo, removê-lo ou tocá-lo. Entre em contato com a SMS para receber orientações e realizar a notificação", diz a pasta em nota à TV TEM.

articles.title: 37% avaliam Congresso como ruim ou péssimo, aponta Datafolha | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa ouviu 2.002 eleitores em 125 municípios entre 22 e 23 de setembro. Avaliação negativa se manteve no mesmo patamar de maio.
articles.summary: Pesquisa ouviu 2.002 eleitores em 125 municípios entre 22 e 23 de setembro. Avaliação negativa se manteve no mesmo patamar de maio.
articles.body:
Cúpula do Senado Federal e prédio do Congresso Nacional durante o amanhecer. — Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

O trabalho dos senadores e deputados federais é considerado ruim ou péssimo por 37% dos eleitores brasileiros , segundo pesquisa Datafolha divulgada neste sábado (26).

➡️O Datafolha entrevistou 2.002 eleitores com 16 anos ou mais em 125 municípios de todo o país, nos dias 22 e 23 de setembro de 2026. A margem de erro máxima é de dois pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos.

De acordo com a pesquisa, 18% avaliam o desempenho dos parlamentares como ótimo ou bom , enquanto 40% consideram o trabalho regular. A parcela que não soube responder é de 6%.

Os resultados são semelhantes aos registrados na pesquisa anterior, realizada em maio. Naquele levantamento, 37% avaliavam o Congresso como ruim ou péssimo, 15% como ótimo ou bom e 43% como regular.

A avaliação do Congresso também variou de acordo com a intenção de voto para a Presidência da República.

A aprovação é maior entre os eleitores que declararam intenção de votar em Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), entre os quais 22% consideram o desempenho dos deputados e senadores ótimo ou bom .

Já entre os eleitores de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), o percentual é de 15%.

A pesquisa também avaliou como os parlamentares são avaliados a partir do recorte de gênero, renda e região do Brasil.

A classificação do trabalho como ruim ou péssimo é maior entre homens (43%) do que entre mulheres (32%).

A avaliação também é pior entre aqueles que declararam renda acima de cinco salários mínimos por mês (51%) – entre os que recebem até dois salários mínimos, fica em 30%.

Entre as regiões, o Sudeste é a área em que os deputados e senadores tem a avaliação mais negativa, com 41% afirmando que o trabalho é ruim ou péssimo. Na sequência aparecem Centro-Oeste e Norte (38%), Sul (36%) e Nordeste (32%).

Já os que enxergam como ótimo ou bom são 16% no Sudeste e no Sul, 21% no Nordeste e 17% no Centro-Oeste e no Norte.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: veja como foi o dia dos candidatos ao Governo do Maranhão neste sábado (26) | G1
articles.standfirst: Veja como foram as atividades de campanha de André Luís, Dimas Cassimiro, Eduardo Braide, Felipe Camarão, Orleans Brandão, Reginaldo Lima, Roberto Rocha e Saulo Arcangeli.
articles.summary: Veja como foram as atividades de campanha de André Luís, Dimas Cassimiro, Eduardo Braide, Felipe Camarão, Orleans Brandão, Reginaldo Lima, Roberto Rocha e Saulo Arcangeli.
articles.body:
Os candidatos ao Governo do Maranhão cumpriram compromissos de campanha neste sábado (26), em diferentes municípios do estado. André Luis (Missão), Orleans Brandão (MDB) e Reginaldo Lima (PCB), além dos demais candidatos, apresentaram propostas voltadas para mulheres, idosos, pessoas com deficiência e outros grupos vulneráveis.

O primeiro turno das eleições será realizado no dia 4 de outubro. Já o segundo turno, caso necessário, está marcado para 25 de outubro.

Veja quem são os candidatos a governador no Maranhão — Foto: Montagem g1

Dimas Casimiro, do Partido da Causa Operária (PCO), não informou a agenda de campanha neste sábado (26).

Eduardo Braide, do Partido Social Democrático (PSD), participou de uma carreata neste sábado (26) pela manhã, em Colinas e São Domingos. À tarde, o candidato participou de uma carreata em Tuntum. À noite, cumpriu agenda com uma caminhada em Barra do Corda.

Felipe Camarão, do Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), gravou o programa eleitoral neste sábado (26) pela manhã. À tarde e à noite, o candidato participou de uma carreata em Açailândia.

Roberto Rocha, do Partido Renovador Trabalhista Brasileiro (PRTB), recebeu uma liderança política neste sábado (26) pela manhã, em Chapadinha. À tarde, participou de uma carreata na cidade. À noite, viajou para Buriticupu.

Saulo Arcangeli, do Partido Socialista dos Trabalhadores Unificado (PSTU), fez panfletagem neste sábado (26) pela manhã no comércio de rua próximo à Feirinha da Vila Lobão e na Rua do Comércio, em Imperatriz.

À tarde, participou de um seminário sobre patrimônio cultural na Umaçul e fez panfletagem na Feirinha do Bonsucesso, também em Imperatriz.

André Luiz, do Missão, cumpriu agenda pela manhã no Centro de São Luís. O candidato caminhou pela Praça Deodoro, conversou com eleitores, ouviu demandas e apresentou propostas para o governo do Maranhão.

Entre os temas abordados, André Luiz falou sobre políticas públicas voltadas para mulheres, idosos, pessoas com deficiência e pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade social.

“Nosso projeto para o governo do estado do Maranhão é sempre ir na raiz dos nossos problemas para garantir direito às mulheres idosos, pessoas com deficiência e em vulnerabilidade social. Nós precisamos entender que o governo não vai conseguir fazer tudo. Nós precisamos entender que é a banalização da paternidade, que tem causado muitos problemas na nossa sociedade. Hoje, lamentavelmente, 70 a 80% dos homens abandonam suas mulheres quando os filhos têm algum tipo de deficiência e por nós do Partido Missão apresentarmos medidas profundas para resolver as chagas da nossa sociedade. Nós fomos reconhecidos pelo Jornal Internacional de Economist como o único programa que pode fazer o Brasil e o Maranhão se desenvolver de fato, colocando pressão para que os pais assumam a sua responsabilização, não só na questão financeira, mas também na questão da presença e cuidado com suas famílias, porque é isso que vai cuidar das nossas casas”, afirmou o candidato.

Orleans Brandão, do Movimento Democrático Brasileiro (MDB), realizou uma carreata pela manhã nas cidades de Bacabal e Lago do Junco. À tarde, participou de uma reunião política em Lago dos Rodrigues e, em seguida, fez uma caminhada em São Luís Gonzaga. À noite, cumpriu agenda em Lago da Pedra.

O candidato apresentou propostas para ampliar políticas públicas de assistência e inclusão no Maranhão, com ações voltadas para mulheres, idosos, pessoas com deficiência e famílias de pessoas com transtorno do espectro autista (TEA).

“Primeiro eu quero trabalhar pelas mulheres em todo o estado do Maranhão. Então vou levar a Casa da Mulher Maranhense, que é grande centro de acolhimento. Nós temos 6 hoje espalhadas pelo Estado e eu quero levar para 18 regionais. Eu também vou criar a Secretaria da Inclusão, a secretaria que vai atender todos os públicos do estado do Maranhão e nela a gente vai colocar programas como Travessia, que tem ajudado muita gente a ir para o seu trabalho. Vou criar a Casa do Idoso, chegando em vários locais do nosso estado. Vai ser também espaço de acolhimento para a nossa melhor idade. E é claro, o Centro TAS que eu vou espalhar por todo o estado do Maranhão, levando atendimento não só a criança e ao adolescente, mas a toda a família. A capacitação profissional para essa mãe da criança com o transtorno do espectro autista, para que ela possa sim trabalhar, fazer uma grande parceria com o governo federal para a gente chegar em quem mais precisa”, afirmou o candidato.

Reginaldo Lima, do Partido Comunista Brasileiro (PCB), fez campanha pela manhã em Itapecuru-Mirim. O candidato visitou comunidades quilombolas da região e, em Filipa, esteve na casa de eleitores, onde ouviu demandas e apresentou propostas do plano de governo.

O candidato, que tem base de campanha em Imperatriz, onde nasceu e mora, passou a semana visitando territórios quilombolas, que também são base eleitoral do candidato a vice, Bartolomeu Moreira.

Durante as visitas, Reginaldo Lima falou sobre propostas para mulheres, idosos e pessoas com deficiência.

“As mulheres, os idosos, as pessoas com deficiência terão total prioridade, porque aqui no governo do PCB trataremos de políticas públicas de inclusão para os idosos, para as pessoas com deficiência e para as mulheres. Iremos ampliar as casas de proteção a essas mulheres, porque aqui no Maranhão ainda está no ranking de feminicídio. Não basta apenas papel. Basta que o Estado também esteja com essas mulheres, protegendo através de políticas públicas. Então, no governo do PCB trataremos dessa questão com muito carinho, o idoso, a mulher, as pessoas com deficiência”, afirmou o candidato.

articles.title: Proibição das bets no futebol: Governo e clubes devem discutir medida | G1
articles.standfirst: Objetivo do encontro é calcular os impactos da proibição das apostas no futebol. Sites e aplicativos de bets deverão sair do ar até 6 de outubro.
articles.summary: A proibição das bets no futebol motiva reunião entre governo e clubes para avaliar o fim dos patrocínios de casas de apostas a partir de outubro.
articles.body:
Em meio à reação negativa dos clubes brasileiros a Medida Provisória que proibiu as bets no país, o governo federal planeja uma reunião com representantes dos times para entender as demandas abertas com o corte dos sites de apostas. A previsão é de que o encontro aconteça na próxima semana.

O encontro está sendo costurado pelo ministro do Esporte, Paulo Henrique Perna Cordeiro, que antecipou que o governo pretende ouvir os times e avaliar como pode contribuir para evitar possíveis prejuízos.

Apesar do valor expressivo, Paulo Henrique afirma que "o futebol sempre viveu sem as bets".

Ministro dos Esportes, Paulo Henrique Perna Cordeiro — Foto: Henrique Barrios/Ministério do Esporte

Grandes times se posicionaram contra a medida do governo. Numa publicação que gerou críticas da torcida, o Flamengo afirmou que "não se pode criar uma regra, levar empresas e instituições a assumir compromissos com base nela e, de um dia para o outro, mudar todo o marco regulatório".

O clube carioca recebe R$ 268,5 milhões por temporada de um site de apostas. O Fluminense, que recebe R$ 52 milhões no mesmo padrão de contrato, defendeu um "período de transição adequado".

O mesmo prazo valerá para a retirada de peças e ações de publicidade e remoção de marcas vinculadas a contratos de patrocínio. Antes da confirmação da proibição, as empresas de apostas on-line pressionaram os clubes com notificações sobre a possibilidade de rescisão dos contratos.

Governo anuncia proibição das bets no Brasil 3 anos após ter regulamentado as empresas de apostas — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A proposta ainda precisa ser aprovada pelos parlamentares e sancionada pelo presidente da República para começar a valer.

Explorar ou operar as chamadas 'apostas de quota fixa', por qualquer meio, passará a ser crime punido com reclusão de 4 a 6 anos, além de multa. A punição será aplicada mesmo que o agente tenha autorização de uma autoridade estrangeira.

articles.title: ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes
articles.summary: Trump tries to dominate at the UN as his approval ratings plummet and even some Republicans stray from the script
articles.body:
Donald Trump stood before the United Nations on Tuesday and threatened to "annihilate" Iran . Yet even as the most powerful man on the planet flexed his military muscles, he was powerless to keep the gravitational pull of domestic politics at bay.

Heading into the UN building in New York , the US president was questioned by Kaitlan Collins , an anchor at CNN , which he had banned from the White House before a judge ruled against him. "I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me," the 80-year-old snapped. "You should not be here covering me."

The lashing-out was a reminder that even Trump, who has expanded executive power and dominated the national consciousness, finds some things beyond his control. Indeed, 20 months into his second term, there is a widening gap between the president's self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence.

Federal courts are reining him in. Congressional Republicans are straying from the script. Poll numbers are tumbling to historic depths , driven by persistent inflation, rising fuel costs and an increasingly unpopular war in Iran. For the first time since his improbable political resurrection, Trump's aura of authority is fading.

Rick Wilson , a longtime Republican strategist, prophesied: "This is the beginning of the end. This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he's been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter."

Trump's self-belief never wavers. He faced four criminal cases and two assassination attempts before winning the 2024 election. He has lived by a mantra of "it will all work out well in the end" while his supporters wear hats that state: "Trump was right about everything."

Yet he has had a rough month. The Federal Reserve defied him on interest rates. The supreme court blocked his administration's attempt to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots for November's midterm elections. One judge prevented him adding his name to the Kennedy Center, prompting him to threaten the national arts complex with demolition; another judge blocked his ban on three news outlets from the White House grounds, ordering the administration to "immediately return, reinstate and restore" their access.

Now even Trump's dependable power base, the Republican party, is showing cracks amid fears that he will cost them seats in November. In Florida, his home state, gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds quietly scrubbed most Trump references from his campaign website, while the congresswoman María Elvira Salazar ran campaign advertisements openly declaring that federal immigration enforcement had gone "too far" and asserting that Latino voters "feel betrayed".

Wilson, a co-founder of the Lincoln Project , an anti-Trump group, sees a herd mentality among congressional Republicans and compares the current mood to a wildlife documentary.

"It needs a David Attenborough voiceover," he said. "It's like the gazelles wandering the savannah. They're sniffing the wind now and they smell something in the wind. They know it's a predator but they don't know what to do about it yet. What they haven't realised is that the predator has been among them all along. The risk factor that they face now is Trump."

For nearly a decade, elected Republicans maintained a posture of submission, fearful of drawing a primary challenger or a scathing post on Truth Social . But with the elections looming and control of Congress hanging in the balance, self-preservation is rapidly overriding loyalty to the president.

Wilson said: "Now it's reached the point where the magic doesn't work any more. There's no political upside from a president who is at 29% approval rating in some polls, has presided over a disastrous war, and has ended up raising energy prices and food prices – all the things that they can't spin away.

" The voters now have very much put that together. They associate the war with Trump. They associate the gas prices with Trump. They associate the grocery prices with Trump."

This creates a vicious circle, Wilson argues. "The more he becomes a liability, the more he acts out. The more he demands loyalty from people and doesn't get it, the more he demands loyalty from people and doesn't get it. Everything was handed to him for a decade by that party and, now that they're paying the price, they've decided this has got a little too hairy."

Faced with shrinking authority and a hostile economic landscape, Trump has reverted to his trusted playbook: manufacturing spectacle, picking cultural fights and raging against the press. His recent decision to ban the news outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House campus following critical coverage was viewed by critics not as a display of strength, but a symptom of deep frustration.

The administration rejects such charges and insists that the president's agenda is succeeding. Davis Ingle , a White House spokesperson, said in an email: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.

"The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs, and sent Americans' 401(k)s climbing to record highs," he added. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction."

But the trend lines are only set to worsen for Trump. If Democrats gain control of the House of Representatives, they plan to launch investigations into how he has allegedly abused his office to enrich his family, grant favours to supporters, hollow out the federal government and carry out expensive construction projects. The attention economy, meanwhile, will inexorably shift to the 2028 presidential race and the question of succession.

Bill Galston , a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, said the inevitable shift of focus toward potential candidates – such as the vice-president, JD Vance, or the secretary of state, Marco Rubio – will be cause for friction.

"Nothing will drive him crazier than the shift of the spotlight away from him," said Galston, a former domestic policy adviser to Bill Clinton. "The prospect of passing the torch, giving up the spotlight, is intensely painful for him. It's his oxygen. Will he be able to breathe, spiritually and emotionally speaking, without it? "

Trump is not the first president to run into trouble after winning re-election. From Richard Nixon's Watergate downfall to Clinton's impeachment and George W Bush's quagmire in Iraq, second terms have historically served as the graveyard of presidential ambition.

Allan Lichtman, author of a new book, Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation , calls it "the second term curse". He noted: "Second terms have been remarkably difficult for presidents."

Lichtman, a history professor at American University in Washington, believes that Trump is driven by two things: money and glory. "He cannot stand not being the centre of attention and that's dangerous," he said. "I don't care much about his verbal lashing-out; I don't think that helps him at all. But who knows what crazy things he might do to reassert attention on him? And that's frightening.

"Never underestimate the power of the president. Just because Republicans are criticising him, his poll numbers are low, prospects for Republicans look dim, doesn't mean he doesn't have enormous power – and he is certainly quite willing to use that power unconstrained. He doesn't care about the courts and doesn't care about the Congress."

From this perspective, Trump's last refuge will be the unchecked use of executive authority, a politicised justice department and a sweeping pardon power. With nothing to lose in his final two years, he could go out all guns blazing.

Charlie Sykes , a conservative author and broadcaster, said: "Donald Trump fears irrelevance more than anything and he'll rage against it as long as he can. The notion that he will go quietly would be incredibly naive.

"We're headed for a collision between a lame duck who has no respect for the constitutional norms and an opposition that may have some power to hold him accountable. The paradox is the weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets."

articles.title: Rising prices, plunging ratings, lingering war: Trump's dinner plate is full
articles.summary: Since Labor Day, Trump traveled to Ireland and the United Nations, and hosted China's president, while voters say the cost of living is a top concern.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump's three-day visit with Chinese President Xi Jinping was filled with pomp and circumstance: a red-carpet arrival, a tour of the National Archives and a state dinner of yellow squash velouté and sesame crusted sea bass.

But the hearty welcome left a bad taste in the mouth of the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

"Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker said on the Senate floor Sept. 22.

Chinese President Xi arrives in US for state visit hosted by Trump

Wicker, one of a growing number of Republicans who have publicly disagreed with the president, may also strike a chord with voters who have told pollsters that the cost of living will be their top priority in the upcoming elections. Lopsided majorities have disapproved of Trump's handling of foreign affairs and the economy.

Trump has pledged to campaign heavily during the month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections in about three-dozen competitive races, including traditional Republican territory in Alaska and Texas. "In some cases, you can be losing by a lot and we'll bring you over the line," Trump told Republicans at a Rose Garden dinner Sept. 2.

But since Labor Day, the traditional start of the campaign season, Trump has focused on foreign affairs. He traveled to Ireland on Sept. 12 and 13 for a meeting with the prime minister and a golf tournament. And he spoke at the United Nations on Sept. 22 , threatening to "annihilate" Iran and predicting the failure of Cuba's government.

Meanwhile, high gas prices and record-high diesel costs spurred some Republican candidates to distance themselves from Trump by calling for an end to the war on Iran or removing references to Trump's endorsement from campaign websites .

John Pitney Jr., a politics professor at Claremont McKenna College in California, said involvement in foreign affairs isn't a problem by itself for Trump because people expect presidents to manage foreign policy. But Trump's problem is what he says about foreign affairs, Pitney said.

"In May, he said he was focused on Iran and didn't care 'even a little bit' about the war's economic impact," Pitney told USA TODAY. "That hurts. The war itself hurts. People get a reminder of the cost every time they drive past a gas station."

Trump's hosting of China's Xi Jinping draws criticism from key Senate Republican

Trump said he had "a very good meeting" with Xi on Sept. 24 without elaborating. Key topics of conversation were about technology, security and artificial intelligence .

"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said.

"A lot of very positive things happened," Trump said Sept. 25 while hosting Xi for tea in the White House's Red Room, adding that farmers would be happy without elaborating. "Great things for both countries. It's been just very, very productive."

But Wicker said he hoped Trump would put the pressure on Xi over multiple issues "while the servers are switching from chardonnay to cabernet at the fancy state dinner." Wicker said Trump should press Xi on whether China provided Iran with satellite imagery that led to the deaths of American troops, harassment of Filipino fishermen and the status of Taiwan.

Asked about Wicker's comments, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters it is vital for the leaders of the world's two largest economies and militaries to meet.

"The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible," Rubio said at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 23 . "It's outrageous."

Trump has argued that any hardship to the economy is worth the price of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. He predicted oil prices would fall sharply as soon as the war ends. Trump told reporters Sept. 25 while touring the National Archives with Xi that they had discussed the war with Iran.

"I think we're going to do great," Trump said.

Voters disapprove of Trump's handling of economy, foreign affairs: polls

Trump's approval rating fell to ​32% – the lowest of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran ‌war, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll of 1,277 adults nationwide released Sept. 21.

Just ​17% of respondents approved of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which the poll found was the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November. Some 82% of poll respondents – including nine in ​ten Democrats and three-quarters of Republicans – said the ​conflict would likely go on for ⁠an "extended period of time."

The cost of groceries, gas and healthcare rank as top pain points for rural voters, according to an Associated Press poll, in partnership with KFF .

Nearly seven in 10 rural voters supported Trump in the 2024 election. But about two-thirds of rural voters were "very" or "somewhat" worried about being able to afford gas or healthcare, compared to about one-third who were not, according to the survey of more than 2,000 registered voters surveyed over two weeks in late August.

About 60% of voters were concerned about the cost of groceries or monthly utilities, compared to 40% who weren't, the poll found.

About two-thirds of registered voters disapproved of Trump's handling of the economy and the war with Iran, according to a Quinnipiac University poll that surveyed 970 registered voters Sept. 3 to 6.

About 60% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of Russia's war with Ukraine, trade with Canada and foreign policy.

"While neither (party) gets high marks generally, the Democrats are judged more empathetic when it comes to the concerns of voters," Tim Malloy, a Quinnipiac University polling analyst.

Trump touts investment in US and lower crime rate

Trump gave significant attention to domestic issues during his speech Sept. 22 to the United Nations General Assembly . He promoted investment in the United States, a lower crime rate and heightened border security. He has argued that eliminating taxes on overtime, tips and Social Security benefits, and negotiating lower prices for prescription drugs, should make for a winning ticket in November.

"America is rising. Our nation is growing. Our power is expanding," Trump said. "Our country is doing better than ever before, and our future is very, very bright."

But foreign affairs dominated the speech and headlines focused on his threat to "annihilate" Iran, his prediction that Cuba's government "will fall" and that the "spoils" of Venezuelan oil from removing that country's president "belong to the victor."

"While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them," Trump said. "While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world."

Some GOP candidates distance themselves from Trump over Iran

Some fellow Republicans have lost patience with the war that began Feb. 28. Four Senate Republicans −Alaska's Lisa Murkowski, North Carolina's Thom Tillis, Kentucky's Rand Paul and Maine's Susan Collins −supported a resolution Sept. 24 to end the war, although the measure failed .

Trump initially said the war would last weeks. After six months, he predicted it would end soon after the Nov. 3 midterm elections for Congress.

Fuel prices are up significantly because of Iran's threat to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Higher costs for diesel fuel ripple through the economy because of the higher cost of transportation.

Gas prices averaged $4.49 on Sept. 25 , compared to $2.87 in late January , according to AAA. Diesel fuel averaged $6.50 per gallon on Sept. 25, after breaking $6 on Sept. 11 for the first time ever.

Trump has said higher fuel costs are "a small price to pay" for preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

But former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Michigan, who is campaigning to succeed Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, said on social media Sept. 21 and in a television ad that the Iran war needs to end.

"The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly," Rogers said in the ad, which features his first name in red and last name in blue.

Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who is campaigning to succeed GOP Sen. Joni Ernst, said on social media Sept. 21 that Iowans shouldn't have to foot the bill for the Iran war with higher grocery prices. But she also voted four times against resolutions to end the war immediately .

"Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran," Hinson said.

Both candidates supported suspending the gas tax and diesel exports.

Fed raises interest rates days after Trump trip to Ireland

Another setback to Trump's domestic priorities came days after he returned from a trip to Ireland, when the Federal Reserve Bank raised interest rates Sept. 16 for the first time since July 2023.

Trump traveled to Ireland on Sept. 12 and 13 to meet Taoiseach Micheal Martin and attend the Irish Open golf tournament at his resort in Doonbeg. He advocated Irish reunification and ended tariffs on Irish whiskey, which he'd imposed.

Trump had earlier appointed a new chair, Kevin Warsh, to the Federal Reserve Bank's board and demanded lower interest rates. But the board voted Sept. 16 to raise rates for the first time since 2023.

Rep. Jason Smith, R-Missouri, who heads the Ways and Means Committee, which oversees taxes, echoed Trump in arguing that "interest rates should be coming down, not going up."

"American workers, families, and small businesses have waited long enough for relief from high borrowing costs that make it harder to buy a home, start a business, or get ahead," Smith said in a statement Sept. 16.

But the Fed typically raises rates to tame inflation by making borrowing more expensive, which can lead to less demand and eventually lower prices. The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index, a key measure of underlying inflation , posted its largest increase in four months on Sept. 11. Mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time in a year, making it harder to buy houses.

Trump told reporters in Ireland on Sept. 13 that the country "should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world," no matter what the Federal Reserve's data indicates about inflation and the economy.

"I know more about formulas than anybody, and with the best credit in the world, we make other countries rich," Trump said.

articles.title: House Democrats plan vast oversight of Trump administration. Impeachment is an option
articles.summary: House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda, with investigations of President Donald Trump, his family and his administration if the party sweeps c...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda, with investigations of President Donald Trump , his family and his administration if the party sweeps control of the chamber from Republicans in the November elections.

The undertaking is as robust as it is daunting, spanning several House committees. With majority power comes bigger budgets and staff, and the ability to investigate, subpoena and potentially course-correct what the Democrats say are widespread corruption and abuses of power. Impeachment of the Republican president and Cabinet officials is not off the table.

"There is a cost to the American people of the out-of-control corruption," said Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats win control at the Capitol.

"If folks have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people or screwing over the American people," Jeffries said, "we are going to hold the crooks accountable."

Congress has enormous ability to conduct oversight of the executive branch as part of its power as a coequal branch of government, and a road map for the Democratic-run investigations has already been set by the almost daily letters lawmakers send to the administration and in amicus court filings.

Democrats are asking about the money-making by Trump and his family, whose wealth has grown dramatically since he returned to the White House in January 2025. They are investigating the potential civil rights violations of Americans killed protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and of detained immigrants being deported to faraway countries . They have fought the closing of the Kennedy Center , launched investigations into private funding of the America at 250 celebrations and tracked the shuttering of federal operations, including the U.S. Agency for International Development.

New questions emerge daily, including the Trump family's recent acknowledgment that a weekend wedding party for the president's son Donald Trump Jr. was partly funded by a Russian oligarch , with reportedly close ties to the Kremlin.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is in line to become the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, characterized the issues involved as "gargantuan."

"We need to zero in quickly on the forms of systemic corruption that have cost the public huge amounts of money," Raskin told The Associated Press, "and where there are legislative cures available."

Trump impeachments made history then. Could it happen again?

Jeffries will almost certainly be under pressure from the far left to move more swiftly to articles of impeachment against Trump, who during his first became the first president to be twice impeached by the House. Both times , he was acquitted by the Senate.

Impeaching the president a third time may not hold the currency that it once did. Democrats will more likely focus their impeachment efforts on Cabinet members. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth already faces articles of impeachment from a Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky , over his leadership at the Pentagon and his management of the Iran war.

"We haven't ruled anything out," Jeffries said recently about the tools available to Congress, "and we haven't ruled anything in."

The White House is likely to play hardball if confronted with investigations, and Democrats are bracing for an administration that potentially ignores subpoenas or refuses to turn over paperwork that lawmakers are demanding.

The Democrats are also reaching beyond the administration into various corporate and business entities for potential wrongdoing.

'We'll act like the Congress,' says one Democrat in line to lead a committee

Ranking Democratic lawmakers who are in line to lead committees if power shifts are beginning to chart the investigations they plan to tackle.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat now on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings , the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and ICE operations.

"We're already doing work," Garcia told the AP.

He also mentioned the Department of Health and Human Services under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , as well as broader allegations of corporate corruption.

The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, whose jurisdiction includes the State Department, said the committee plans to investigate Trump's international dealings, including around the Iran war .

He expects the committee will also look into the administration's Venezuela operations — from the military strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific waters to the U.S. partnership with a private company to develop and access the South American country's oil.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat at the Natural Resources Committee, which overseas the Interior Department and its National Park Service operations, has begun digging into Trump's "vanity projects," including the demolition of the White House's East wing for a new ballroom and the president's proposed arch .

Huffman and other committee members have also been eyeing the Trump family's role in various minerals deals.

At the committee's last session before lawmakers recessed to campaign for the midterm elections, Huffman said that if Democrats take charge, he plans to call witnesses, put them under oath and follow the evidence where it leads.

"When people ask what will we do," he said he responds, "My answer is simple. We'll use those tools. We'll act like the Congress."
