articles.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump rejects Iran deal after week of high-stakes meetings; GOP clammers to keep Congress
articles.summary: President Trump rejected a new seven-day proposal from Iran Saturday morning to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt military operations in the ongoing conflict between Tehran and the U.S. “They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” the president told reporters at the White House. “I like making a deal, too, but…
articles.body:
President Trump rejected a new seven-day proposal from Iran Saturday morning to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt military operations in the ongoing conflict between Tehran and the U.S.

“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” the president told reporters at the White House. “I like making a deal, too, but that deal would not be acceptable.”

The president is under heightened pressure ahead of the midterm elections to bring the monthslong war to a conclusion amid rising energy prices tied to the closure of the strait, a major oil trading corridor, and rising public discontent with these U.S. military operations.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian sat down with CBS News’s Margaret Brennan this week to discuss the ongoing conflict. His interview with the network will air on “Face the Nation” this Sunday.

Additionally, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi — who has led the Iranian delegation’s negotiations to reopen the strait — will appear on NBC News’s “Meet the Press .”

Trump’s job approval rating has taken a hit amid the Iran war, sinking to a career low of 32 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos survey released this week. Only 17 percent of the poll’s respondents approved of the way the president has handled rising living costs, a top issue for voters this election cycle.

Some Republicans are concerned this conflict could hurt their chances at retaining power in Congress in November, as the president repeatedly calls for Americans to cast their vote as if he is “on the ballot.”

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), a strong supporter of the president, will join “Face the Nation” on Sunday to discuss the GOP’s strategy less than six weeks out from the midterms.

This week, Trump delivered a speech at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York before bilateral meetings with several world leaders, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. On the sidelines, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, met with members of the Iranian delegation.

The president strongly defended his handling of the Iran war during his remarks and urged nations to join the U.S. in “the complete economic isolation of Iran.”

“They were the bully of the Middle East, but they are the bully no more,” he said. “From the first day I entered the political arena, I’ve been unwavering. I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz will join both “Meet the Press” and CNN’s “State of the Union” this Sunday.

Later last week, the president rolled out the red carpet this week for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s first U.S. state visit in over a decade. The two leaders participated in a lavish state dinner , toured Trump’s updates to the White House grounds and exchanged gifts .

While the pair discussed issues like artificial intelligence development and Taiwan, the summit produced scant policy announcements.

Trump has brushed aside calls to curb the development of advanced AI amid concerns about the potential dangers posed by this technology, citing competition with China.

On Friday, the president said he had a “very productive meeting” with Xi, in which the two global leaders discussed this issue.

“Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

David Perdue, the U.S. a mbassador to China, will appear on Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday” to discuss Xi’s White House visit.

The ranking member on the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), is scheduled to join “Face the Nation” on Sunday.

See the full list of guests on the Sunday morning news shows below:

NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday”: Rep. Rick Crawford (R-Ark.), Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.)

CBS News’s “Face the Nation”: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Taiwan Ambassador to the U.S. Alexander Yui, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.)

CNN’s “State of the Union”: UN Ambassador Mike Waltz, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.)

Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday”: U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, NASA astronaut Chris Williams

NBC News’s “Meet the Press”: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, UN Ambassador Mike Waltz, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates

Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures”: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.), Rep. Jason Smith (R-Mo.), retired Lt. Gen. Keith Kellogg

ABC News’s “This Week”: Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Attorney General Todd Blanche, Cook Political Report political analyst Charlie Cook

articles.title: What Is a ‘Pocket Rescission’? Inside Trump’s Move to Cancel $810 Million in Federal Funding
articles.summary: The Trump Administration is seeking to claw back spending approved for programs serving immigrants, minority groups, and children.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is seeking to cancel almost $1 billion in federal funding, sidestepping congressional approval and earning criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Using a controversial move known as a "pocket rescission," Trump said he wanted to nullify $810 million in spending that Congress had approved for programs and agencies, much of which would serve immigrants, minorities, and children.

Over half of the cuts would land on the Health and Human Services (HHS) Department's Office of Refugee Resettlement, according to a request sent to House Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday. It said that rescinding the funds is "consistent with the Administration's goal of ending the use of Federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens, putting Americans first."

In a statement accompanying the request, the Trump Administration also called the funds "wasteful" and "harmful."

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog, has asserted, however, that the move is an illegal sidestepping of the constitutionally protected separation of powers—chiefly, Congress's power of the purse.

A "pocket rescission" is not a formal or legal term; it was coined to reference a " pocket veto ," a process in which a bill fails to become law because the President does not sign it within 10 days and Congress's adjournment prevents its return. Similarly, the "pocket rescission" aims to withdraw allocated funding without direct congressional intervention.

The timing is important when it comes to pocket rescissions. In order to be fully effective, this "occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations," according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).

The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), helmed by Director Russell Vought, submitted the requests Friday and holds that the move is valid under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act (ICA).

The Impoundment Control Act was created in response to President Richard Nixon's heavy use of impoundments to achieve his policy goals. It has since been used to limit or regulate a president's ability to control spending that has already been appropriated by building in 45 days of continuous congressional session. During this time, Congress is meant to review a President's rescission requests and either approve them or see the funds released as planned.

Trump's request to cancel $810 million in funding, however, came just five days before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, all but ensuring that Congress will not have time to review the proposal in full or prevent the cuts from going into effect.

It is not the first time Trump has used this strategy to thwart spending attempts. He submitted a request on Aug. 28, 2025, to cancel $4.9 billion in foreign aid funds approved by Congress, including $3.2 billion that had been allocated to USAID . Although the move was contested, the Supreme Court last year stayed a lower court injunction requiring roughly $4 billion covered by the rescission request to be obligated.

The GAO claims that the move is illegal, writing on its website that this application of the ICA would "cede Congress's power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds."

"If Congress wanted a president to have that authority, it would need to change the law," it continues.

Zachary Price, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, says that the move is an "abuse" of the ICA.

"It's perverse to read that as, instead, creating this mechanism for unilaterally canceling funds," Price tells TIME, adding that this interpretation is not supported by a lot of "historical practice."

The maneuver seeks to withhold the funds until they expire at the end of the fiscal year, leaving Congress little time to respond.

In this case, Price says, it further showcases how the ICA is being manipulated.

The government "shouldn't have a lot of money left over at the end of the fiscal year if you've been spending it as you go in the way the statute contemplates," he says.

He also points out that the American government is distinctly separated into three branches, with Congress, sitting in the legislative branch, being given the power to pass legislation—or, in this case, cancel funds that have already been appropriated. It has been explicitly separated from the authority of the executive branch and the President.

Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, says it even plainer than Price: "The administration has picked a bunch of things that they hate, and they say, 'Well, we're just not going to do those.'"

The Supreme Court's intervention last year did not constitute a ruling on the authority of pocket rescissions, meaning that the Trump Administration's latest use of the tactic could face new legal challenges.

Which federal programs would lose funding and what's at stake?

The largest portion of this year's proposed cuts will target HHS programs providing nonprofit services for refugees and unaccompanied minors. Trump's request would withdraw $567 million from those services.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was also impacted, with a request to cancel funding for nonprofits that provide mental health services and social services to migrants. Another cut targets almost $25 million that had been slated for the Department of Education's Special Programs for Migrant Students.

The Housing and Urban Development Department's housing counseling services are also named amid the rescissions; the Trump Administration said that the program included non-governmental organizations with "divisive and DEI-centric agendas."

The Trump Administration also aims to cancel $15 million from a Department of Justice office that focuses on reducing racial tensions, in addition to $10 million that had been allocated to the Minority Business Development Agency, which supports minority entrepreneurs.

"I assume that they're picking money to cancel based on some political calculus about what they can get away with," Price says. When looking at the bigger picture, he argues this is just one maneuver in several to "establish stronger executive control over spending."

The move also risks future negotiations in Congress, Price says. He explains that this application of the ICA would make it harder for Democrats and Republicans to compromise over spending if they anticipate that the sitting President will simply swoop in and cancel funding after thoughtful agreements have been reached.

"If the executive branch can come in and effectively impose a more kind of party line view of the spending, then you know why would people agree to the package in the first place?" he asks.

Can Congress stop Trump's pocket rescission?

The rescission has earned blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who believe that the move sidesteps Congress's authority.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, lambasted the move on social media Friday evening , saying she would "work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions."

"This move shows that OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law," Collins said. "OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding."

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, Collins's Democratic counterpart on the Appropriations Committee, called the move "theft from the American people."

"Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because Vought is saying their votes don't count," Murray said in a statement on X.

The August 2025 pocket rescission was challenged in an existing lawsuit brought by nonprofits, including AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, over the Administration's prior foreign aid freeze. In September, the Supreme Court allowed the funds covered by the rescission request to remain withheld while litigation continued. This year, similar lawsuits are likely to emerge—but how they might shape future ICA actions remains to be seen.

According to Kogan, this move sets up a potential battle in Congress to claw back these funds in the next fiscal cycle by reappropriating funds to the same programs.

"One thing that Congress could do is they could say 'I know you illegally didn't spend it this year, but take that money we're going to slap it right back on,'" he says. "That doesn't make [Vought] spend it next year, but it does say that we are going to make sure this money gets out the door, even if it's years late."

articles.title: Trump says he is rolling back Biden-era US fuel economy rules for cars
articles.summary: The US president said he would end a so-called ‘EV mandate’ that steered consumers to electric vehicles.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has announced new fuel economy standards that roll back requirements adopted under his predecessor, arguing they will lower automobile prices and encourage manufacturers to expand production in the US.

In a social media post on Saturday, Trump said the new standards would “TERMINATE” what he called former US President Joe Biden’s “EV (electric vehicle) mandate”, accusing the previous administration of imposing costly requirements on carmakers and steering consumers towards electric vehicles.

“These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car,” Trump wrote.

The changes form part of a broader Trump administration effort to reverse Biden-era policies supporting lower-emission vehicles, increasing the gap between US policy and global trends favouring electric vehicles.

While Trump and US Republicans have used the term “EV mandate” to describe higher fuel efficiency requirements instituted under Biden, a Democrat, there are no federal guidelines or laws that require Americans to buy electric cars or bar the sale of ones powered by petrol.

At the centre are Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards. This system, established by the US Congress in 1975, requires automakers to meet average fuel economy targets across all cars and light trucks they sell, meaning that a brand that sells an inefficient vehicle would also have to sell a more efficient one to help comply with the government’s standards.

Under rules finalised by the Biden administration in 2024, the required fleetwide fuel economy was scheduled to rise from 39.1 miles per gallon (mpg) to about 50.4mpg by 2031. The administration said then the measures would reduce fuel consumption and emissions to combat climate change while helping motorists save money at the pump.

As a result, auto manufacturers have ramped up production of EVs to help meet the Biden-imposed fuel economy requirements. The Republican-controlled US Congress, however, gutted consumer tax incentives last year for electric vehicles as part of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Trump did not provide details regarding what the new fuel economy standards would be. But in December 2025, he announced a proposal that would set the industry fleetwide average for light-duty vehicles at roughly 34.5mpg by 2031, more than 30 percent lower than the Biden-era rule.

In a reposting of Trump’s announcement, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an announcement would be “COMING MONDAY”.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Former Kennedy Center employees claim officials halted repairs months prior to closure
articles.summary: Former Kennedy Center employees accused the iconic performing arts venue’s leadership in a letter to Congress of halting planned waterproofing repairs earlier this year. In the Thursday letter, David Seide, an attorney representing the whistleblowers, shared internal documents which he said challenged the Kennedy Center board’s claims that these leaks warranted the venue’s immediate closure. …
articles.body:
Former Kennedy Center employees accused the iconic performing arts venue’s leadership in a letter to Congress of halting planned waterproofing repairs earlier this year.

In the Thursday letter, David Seide, an attorney representing the whistleblowers, shared internal documents which he said challenged the Kennedy Center board’s claims that these leaks warranted the venue’s immediate closure.

The board, led by President Trump, cited these leaks in its decision last week to temporarily close the center’s main building to assess renovation needs, saying the facility was “unsafe for continued occupancy.”

The New York Times was the first to report on this letter.

Seide said the Kennedy Center’s executive director, Matt Floca, knew about these leakage issues “for years” and canceled planned repairs earlier this year despite receiving $9.3 million from Congress for this renovation.

“In sum, the evidence shows that the New Problems were in fact well known, were not considered to be high priorities and that millions in taxpayer funds were set aside more than a year ago to address them,” Seide wrote.

His letter also alleges Floca diverted congressionally appropriated funds for repairs to make “unplanned cosmetic changes” requested by Trump to repaint the main building’s columns white last year.

The board has directed several other cosmetic changes to the Kennedy Center’s campus under Trump’s leadership, including the temporary addition of the president’s name to the main building’s facade and the removal of a towering sculpture from the center’s grounds

The attorney called on Congress to investigate the matter further.

In a statement shared with The Hill, Floca pushed back on these allegations and said the center’s leadership had become aware of more severe leakage issues in recent months.

“The safety of our patrons, artists, and staff comes first,” Floca said. “The Kennedy Center has known for years that the roof overhang leaked. What we did not know until this summer was how far the damage had spread inside it.”

Floca added that the earlier roof repair plans were delayed because the contractor’s bid was over $500,000 more than the projected cost for this project. He said these fixes are now being addressed within the center’s broader development plan.

“That was a change in the approach to procuring and delivering the work, not a determination that the work was unnecessary,” Floca said.

Seide’s letter was shared with the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, as well as the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), the Senate committee’s top Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center’s board, has led an investigation into allegations of corruption within the iconic performing arts venue.

In a separate Thursday letter , addressed to Floca, the Rhode Island Democrat accused the executive director and the board of making “poor decisions,” calling for answers to the findings in this new whistleblower report by Oct. 8.

“My initial investigation into misconduct at the Center focused on cronyism and corruption, with documents demonstrating considerable excessive and self-serving spending under President Trump’s chairmanship,” Whitehouse wrote.

“The documents that I attach today seem to reveal deeper financial mismanagement,” he continued. “Your failure to respond to my previous requests for financial documents, and the unexplained sudden departure of the CFO, suggest that something is seriously wrong at the Center.”

The new whistleblower claims come amid an ongoing legal challenge to Trump’s changes at the performing arts center brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio member of the center’s board.

Earlier this year, Trump announced plans to close the Kennedy Center for a total of two years for renovations, but a federal judge blocked this effort. The administration has said it could demolish the building and replace it with an open-air performance space if its planned construction is not permitted.

articles.title: Trump says he ended Biden electric vehicle rule, updated fuel economy standards
articles.summary: President Trump announced Saturday he approved new fuel economy standards that eliminate an electric vehicle (EV) mandate introduced under the Biden administration. The 2024 EV mandate aimed to facilitate the transition from gas-powered to EVs by setting new pollution standards for automakers’ vehicle fleets, which were intentionally difficult to meet without introducing new electric or…
articles.body:
President Trump announced Saturday he approved new fuel economy standards that eliminate an electric vehicle (EV) mandate introduced under the Biden administration.

The 2024 EV mandate aimed to facilitate the transition from gas-powered to EVs by setting new pollution standards for automakers’ vehicle fleets, which were intentionally difficult to meet without introducing new electric or low-carbon models. Trump celebrated its elimination in a Truth Social post as a “BIG DAY FOR AMERICAN AUTO WORKERS AND CAR BUYERS!”

“These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America,” the president wrote.

“That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car — Far better than the Environmental Monsters that we were building heretofore,” he continued. “Every Manufacturer, from General Motors to Ford to Stellantis, has called me wanting to build here, and now they can!”

The Trump administration has targeted several Biden-era initiatives directed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions and fossil fuel use.

His announcement comes less than six weeks ahead of the midterm elections, in which Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress amid concerns among voters about rising fuel prices — as well as other living costs — under the Trump administration.

The Sierra Club criticized the president’s decision to roll back these requirements, arguing it will make transportation more expensive for Americans.

Katherine García, the director of the Sierra Club’s “Clean Transportation for All” campaign, vowed to “fight this senseless rollback every step of the way” in a Saturday statement .

“Families already cannot afford the basics, and now Donald Trump wants to make driving more expensive too,” García said.

“Less fuel-efficient cars mean more gas burned, spending more at the pump, and dirtier air in our communities,” she continued. “Americans need relief from high costs, but instead Trump is giving automakers a free pass on pollution and handing families the bill – at the pump and with their health.”

Former Biden Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg similarly slammed the president’s decision to remove these EV standards.

“U.S. manufacturing jobs are down under Trump, including in the auto industry. His strategy failed, and so will this,” he wrote on social media . “Lowering standards will accelerate what he has already been doing: handing the clean tech future to China and forcing Americans to pay more at the pump.”

articles.title: Trump slams reporting on removal of his endorsements from GOP candidate’s website
articles.summary: President Trump criticized the media on Saturday following reports that GOP Rep. Byron Donalds (Fla.) removed several references to the president’s endorsement of his gubernatorial bid from his campaign website. The president slammed this reporting as “Another Fake Story” in a Truth Social post, citing his election wins in Florida during his three presidential campaigns.…
articles.body:
President Trump criticized the media on Saturday following reports that GOP Rep. Byron Donalds (Fla.) removed several references to the president’s endorsement of his gubernatorial bid from his campaign website.

The president slammed this reporting as “Another Fake Story” in a Truth Social post , citing his election wins in Florida during his three presidential campaigns.

“If Florida thought the story that Byron ‘dropped’ me was true, he would lose the Election, and that would be a terrible thing because he’s going to be a fantastic Governor!” Trump wrote.

The gubernatorial candidate’s campaign removed several mentions of the president’s name from its website, including a top banner that encouraged supporters to “chip in to support Trump Endorsed Byron Donalds.”

The homepage now opens with the slogan, “Fighting to defend the Florida dream,” with a cycling list of endorsements below, including that of the president.

The president’s post included a screenshot of Donalds’s response to media reports on these changes, in which the gubernatorial candidate said he was “proud to have” Trump’s endorsement and shared a photo of them together behind the Resolute desk.

The move came as several Republican candidates running in battleground states seek to distance themselves from the Trump administration amid rising public discontent with increased living costs and the ongoing U.S. military operations against Iran.

The president’s criticism of the “Fake News Media” in his Saturday post also followed his recent decision to bar several news outlets from the White House grounds.

“I call them out, but they should really be called out by the Courts, and should not be allowed to enter the White House premises, or Press Room, because they are CORRUPT and DISHONEST!” he wrote on Saturday.

This week, the Trump administration revoked White House press credentials from reporters with MS NOW, CNN and Politico after the president imposed a ban on these outlets “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”

The decision was later overturned after a federal judge ordered the White House to restore access to reporters from these outlets, finding this ban likely violated their constitutional rights.
